extraction.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
extraction.description: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) is a curated subset of 23 challenging BIG-Bench tasks (27 subtasks) for which no prior language model result from Srivastava et al. (2022) outperformed the average human-rater score. The benchmark is used to evaluate chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting versus standard answer-only prompting on large language models.
extraction.creator: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei (Google Research, Stanford University)
extraction.citeAs: Suzgun et al. (2022). Challenging BIG-Bench tasks and whether chain-of-thought can solve them. arXiv:2210.09261.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: BBH was constructed by filtering and curating tasks from the existing BIG-Bench benchmark using a set of criteria including number of subtasks, number of examples, availability of human-rater baselines, evaluation metric type, and model performance relative to human-rater scores. The authors then manually inspected the remaining tasks and excluded those deemed too difficult or outside scope.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some tasks that were added later in the curation process lack human baselines, while other tasks only have the minimum number of examples needed to qualify for submission.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The source data is the BIG-Bench benchmark (Srivastava et al., 2022), a collaborative benchmark with over 200 diverse text-based tasks.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Tasks were filtered by: (1) removing tasks with more than three subtasks, (2) removing tasks with fewer than 103 examples, (3) removing tasks without human-rater baselines, (4) removing tasks that do not use multiple-choice or exact match as the evaluation metric, (5) removing tasks where the best reported model beats the average human-rater score, and (6) removing extremely difficult tasks outside the scope of the work. For all but three tasks, a random subset of 250 evaluation examples was taken.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Chain-of-thought exemplars were manually composed by the authors. Three chain-of-thought exemplars were written for each task in BBH, with 'let's think step-by-step' prepended to all CoT annotations in the few-shot exemplars.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The human-rater performance scores are not fully representative of human performance. The human-evaluation component took almost a year, during which formatting and content of some tasks changed multiple times. Human-raters were allocated a few hours per day and could use external resources such as the Internet. In some cases, task descriptions were hard to follow.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The human-rater performance scores should be interpreted with care as they are not fully representative of human performance. Surpassing average human-rater performance on challenging tasks should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning. Some tasks require domain-specific knowledge or are not practically solvable within twenty minutes.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating and benchmarking large language models, particularly for testing chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot prompting capabilities on challenging tasks requiring multi-step reasoning.

name.evidence: We select a subset of 23 particularly challenging tasks and group them into an evaluation suite referred to as BIG-Bench Hard (BBH), which we make publicly available.

description.evidence: In this paper, we curate BIG-Bench Hard (BBH), a subset of 23 particularly challenging BIG-Bench tasks (27 subtasks) for which no prior result from Srivastava et al. (2022) has outperformed the average human-rater score.

url.evidence: The data, prompts, and the Codex model outputs are all available at https://github.com/suzgunmirac/BIG-Bench-Hard .

creator.evidence: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei — Google Research, Stanford University

inLanguage.evidence: BIG-Bench is a diverse evaluation suite... The benchmark has over 200 diverse text-based tasks in task categories including traditional NLP, mathematics, commonsense reasoning, and question-answering.

isLiveDataset.evidence: We release the data and prompts used in the work, as well as the outputs from the Codex models, to facilitate further research.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: We, therefore, choose a set of criteria (listed in Table 1) to filter BIG-Bench to arrive at a clean, challenging, and tractable subset.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: We analyze BIG-Bench by identifying tasks for which the highest reported model performances are below the average human-rater score... Based on manual inspection of 36 these tasks, we divide them into two categories.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: Given the large number of evaluation tasks in BIG-Bench, the tasks vary in how clean their data and metadata are. For example, some tasks that were added later in the curation process lack human baselines, while other tasks only have the minimum number of examples needed to qualify for submission.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: BIG-Bench is a collaborative benchmark that aims to quantitatively measure the capabilities and limitations of language models (Srivastava et al., 2022, Beyond the Imitation Game Benchmark). The benchmark has over 200 diverse text-based tasks in task categories including traditional NLP, mathematics, commonsense reasoning, and question-answering.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: These filtering criteria result in 78 clean multiple-choice or exact-match tasks... For all but three tasks in BBH, we take a random subset of 250 evaluation examples.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: We manually compose three chain-of-thought exemplars for each task in BBH; all the prompts used are shown in Section C. We prepend 'let's think step-by-step' (Kojima et al., 2022) to all CoT annotations in the few-shot exemplars.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: We manually compose three chain-of-thought exemplars for each task in BBH.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: The human-evaluation component of the benchmark took almost a year, during which the formatting and content of some tasks had been changed multiple times. Human-raters were allocated a few hours per day to solve a sub-sampled evaluation set of a benchmark task, where they could use external resources such as the Internet. In some cases, the task description was hard to follow and could have been better-formulated.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: The above-mentioned factors suggest that the human-rater performance, as well as the results discussed in this work, should be interpreted with care. Therefore, surpassing average human-rater performance score on a set of challenging tasks should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We release the data and prompts used in the work, as well as the outputs from the Codex models, to facilitate further research.
